clue.text: One of Woolf's, certainly not of one's own

definitions.text: One of Woolf's, certainly not of one's own

parts.words: One of Woolf's, certainly not of one's own
parts.note: a Virginia Woolf title with a room in it, but not the essay A Room of One's Own: her 1922 novel named for a young man's lodging

explanation.surface: A reader is pinning down which Virginia Woolf book is meant, ruling out her famous essay.
explanation.walkthrough: Woolf's best-known room is the one in her essay 'A Room of One's Own'; the clue steers away from it to her novel about Jacob Flanders, whose rooms frame the book.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf's third novel takes its title from the student lodgings of its hero, Jacob Flanders.

clue.text: Hardy manager first judge of practical people

indicators.note: the word first here tells us to take the opening letter of each of the four words that follow

explanation.surface: A Hardy novel's manager is the first to judge practical people.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hardy's The Mayor of Casterbridge, Joshua Jopp is the manager Henchard hires after dismissing Farfrae.
explanation.definitionFit: Jopp is the corn-business manager employed by Michael Henchard in Thomas Hardy's The Mayor of Casterbridge.

clue.text: Jargon adds nothing in verse

indicators.note: the answer adds a letter to become a verse unit, so the verse word less that letter is what we enter

parts.note: a canto is a division of a long poem
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Specialist jargon contributes nothing to poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'adds nothing in verse' as: this word, plus O, becomes a verse section. So the answer is CANTO with its O taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: Cant is the private language or slang of a group, much like jargon.

clue.text: Mayflower launched by him in

parts.note: not the Pilgrim Fathers' ship but the Valencian novel Flor de mayo (The Mayflower) of 1895, named after a fishing boat, by a Spanish novelist

explanation.surface: Someone launched the famous Pilgrim ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mayflower suggests the 1620 ship; here it is the English title of Flor de mayo, a novel about Valencian fishermen and their boat by the author of The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse.
explanation.definitionFit: Vicente Blasco Ibáñez, Spanish novelist, published Flor de mayo, translated as The Mayflower, in 1895.

clue.text: Concerning first woman novelist

parts.note: re is the Latin-derived word for about or concerning
Eve is the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: A remark about the first woman to write novels.
explanation.walkthrough: Clara Reeve was an eighteenth-century English novelist, author of The Old English Baron.
explanation.definitionFit: Clara Reeve wrote Gothic fiction, The Old English Baron among it, in the 1770s.

clue.text: Team of players in outbreak of minor chest rash

indicators.note: the letters break out from inside the run of words that follows, so the answer sits within them

explanation.surface: A band of players comes down with a mild rash on the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra is a company of musicians playing together, a team of instrumentalists.

clue.text: Lost vital fluid in the Julian Alps

definitions.meaning: lost blood, past tense of the verb meaning to lose blood
a lake resort in north-west Slovenia sits in the Julian Alps

explanation.surface: Someone lost blood while out in the Julian Alps.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose blood is to bleed, past tense; and Bled is the Slovenian lakeside town in that mountain range.

clue.text: Festival following Juliet's birthday

parts.note: the Nurse in Romeo and Juliet says Juliet turns fourteen on the eve of the August harvest festival of loaves

explanation.surface: A celebration held just after Juliet's birthday.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo and Juliet: 'Come Lammas-eve at night shall she be fourteen.' The festival of 1 August, when loaves from the first harvest were blessed, follows that eve.
explanation.definitionFit: Lammas, 1 August, was the English harvest festival; its season is the period after Juliet's birthday on Lammas Eve.

clue.text: Making out with good taste

definitions.meaning: making out in the sense of perceiving or distinguishing something

explanation.surface: Kissing someone with good taste.
explanation.definitionFit: Discern means perceive, so discerning is making out; and a discerning person has refined judgement.

clue.text: That they are fickle-minded and treacherous is as true as the " (Edgar Allen Poe, A Tale of Jerusalem)

definitions.text: That they are fickle-minded and treacherous is as true as the " (Edgar Allen Poe, A Tale of Jerusalem)

parts.words: That they are fickle-minded and treacherous is as true as the " (Edgar Allen Poe, A Tale of Jerusalem)
parts.note: a quotation to complete: the missing words name the five books of Moses, used as a byword for unquestionable truth

explanation.surface: A line from Poe's story set in besieged Jerusalem, with its final word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the quotation from Poe's 'A Tale of Jerusalem'; the speaker swears by the first five books of the Hebrew Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: The five books of Moses, Genesis to Deuteronomy, are the scripture Poe's speaker invokes as the standard of certainty.

clue.text: Novelist's French friends

definitions.meaning: Kingsley or Martin, father and son British writers
the French word for male friends, plural

explanation.surface: A novelist's French companions.
explanation.definitionFit: Kingsley and Martin are both British novelists of that surname; and the French plural for friends is amis.

clue.text: Fitzgerald's battered inn

parts.note: Edward FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam calls the world 'this batter'd' roadside lodging of the East

explanation.surface: A shabby inn belonging to a man named Fitzgerald.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward FitzGerald, translator of the Rubaiyat: 'Think, in this batter'd Caravanserai / Whose Doorways are alternate Night and Day'. Not F. Scott Fitzgerald.
explanation.definitionFit: An Eastern inn with a courtyard where caravans rest overnight; FitzGerald's verse calls it battered.

clue.text: Survivor among short story tellers

parts.note: the narrator of the Arabian Nights stays alive by telling her husband a tale each night and breaking off before the end

explanation.surface: Someone outlasted the rival authors of short fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: The sultan meant to execute each bride after one night; the narrator of The Thousand and One Nights survived by leaving every story unfinished.
explanation.definitionFit: The storyteller of The Thousand and One Nights escapes execution through her nightly tales.

clue.text: Licence in publishing

parts.note: the Latin 'let it be printed', a formal permission to publish a book

explanation.surface: A permit for issuing books.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for 'let it be printed', it is the official sanction, especially from the Church, allowing a book to be published.

clue.text: "Deuce take me, I have — a pimple here too" (Congreve, The Double Dealer)

definitions.text: "Deuce take me, I have — a pimple here too" (Congreve, The Double Dealer)

parts.words: "Deuce take me, I have — a pimple here too" (Congreve, The Double Dealer)
parts.note: a quotation to complete from Congreve's comedy: the fop Brisk says he has fostered or brought on a spot

explanation.surface: A vain gentleman in a Restoration comedy discovers a spot on his face.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the line from Congreve's The Double Dealer; the missing word, usually meaning heartened, here means fostered a pimple.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means helped along or promoted, as the speaker has helped a blemish grow.

clue.text: Mann cited disaster for him, poor beggar

indicators.note: a disaster leaves things wrecked, so the letters of the two words before are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Thomas Mann pointed to a catastrophe as the cause of a wretched man's ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mann' looks like the German novelist; it only supplies letters. Rearranging MANN CITED gives the beggar.
explanation.definitionFit: A mendicant lives by asking for alms, a beggar, often a friar.

clue.text: Alternate singing apparently opposed to fake

parts.note: anti means against or opposed to
phony means fake, sham

explanation.surface: Responsive singing, it seems, is against fakery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alternate' is an adjective here: singing by two choirs in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Antiphony is responsive chanting in which two groups sing in turn.

clue.text: Bell from London district to continue to play

parts.note: to act is to play a part
on as in carry on, keep going

explanation.surface: A bell from a London suburb keeps on ringing.
explanation.walkthrough: Anne Brontë wrote as Acton Bell, a pen name matching the west London district of Acton.
explanation.definitionFit: Acton Bell was Anne Brontë's pen name, and Acton is a district in west London.

clue.text: "We had roast young suckling pig and drank —" (Hemingway, The Sun also Rises)

definitions.text: "We had roast young suckling pig and drank —" (Hemingway, The Sun also Rises)

parts.words: "We had roast young suckling pig and drank —" (Hemingway, The Sun also Rises)
parts.note: a quotation to complete: in Madrid Jake and Brett drink the red wine of a northern Spanish region

explanation.surface: A meal in Hemingway's Spain: suckling pig and a bottle of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the line from the end of The Sun Also Rises, set at Botín's restaurant in Madrid; the drink is a Spanish red wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Rioja is the red wine of the Spanish region of that name, what Jake drinks in Madrid.

clue.text: Unexpected rage Dante exhibited in restaurant

indicators.note: an unexpected turn of events throws things out of their order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Dante loses his temper without warning in a café.
explanation.definitionFit: An outdoor place serving refreshments, tea and snacks, is a kind of restaurant.

clue.text: Brandy the Spanish quietly stir for French writer

parts.note: marc is a brandy distilled from grape skins
el is the Spanish word for the
p, piano, means quietly in music
to roust is to stir someone up or out of bed

explanation.surface: A French author is told to mix brandy gently, Spanish style.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of In Search of Lost Time was a French novelist.

clue.text: His rage was for life, his appointment with Death

definitions.text: His rage was for life, his appointment with Death

parts.words: His rage was for life, his appointment with Death
parts.note: two titles of one American novelist: A Rage to Live, and Appointment in Samarra, whose title comes from a fable of a meeting with Death

explanation.surface: A man lived passionately until his fated meeting with death.
explanation.walkthrough: John O'Hara wrote A Rage to Live (1949) and Appointment in Samarra (1934), named after the story of a servant who flees Death to Samarra.
explanation.definitionFit: John O'Hara, American novelist, is the author of both A Rage to Live and Appointment in Samarra.

clue.text: Caustic-sounding author of beastly tales

indicators.note: sounding tells us the answer is said like a word for caustic

parts.note: sarky is British slang for sarcastic, caustic

explanation.surface: A writer of animal stories has a biting tone.
explanation.walkthrough: In British speech the R is silent, so SARKY (slang for sarcastic) is said like the pen name of H. H. Munro, whose tales feature wolves, ferrets and a talking cat.
explanation.definitionFit: H. H. Munro, writing as Saki, told stories full of animals such as Tobermory and Sredni Vashtar.

clue.text: Blake's unseen flier

parts.note: in Blake's The Sick Rose an invisible creature flies in the night, in the howling storm

explanation.surface: William Blake's invisible bird.
explanation.walkthrough: Blake: 'O Rose, thou art sick. / The invisible worm / That flies in the night'. A flier you would not expect.
explanation.definitionFit: Blake's poem names an invisible creature that flies in the night to destroy the rose.

clue.text: Got back a robe from Julius Caesar

indicators.note: back says the word just before it is turned round

explanation.surface: Someone retrieved a garment from a production of Julius Caesar.
explanation.definitionFit: Romans such as Caesar wore the toga, a draped woollen robe.

clue.text: Professor puts publicity back on air to get a part in Love's Labour's Lost

definitions.text: a part in Love's Labour's Lost

parts.note: a don is a university teacher
an ad is an advertisement, publicity

indicators.note: back says the two words after it are written in reverse

explanation.surface: An academic runs an advertisement again on the radio to win a Shakespeare role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puts' is only a link, and 'back' turns round only the two words after it. Don Adriano de Armado is the boastful Spanish knight in Love's Labour's Lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Don Adriano de Armado is the fantastical Spanish knight in Shakespeare's Love's Labour's Lost.

clue.text: Went on horseback to find right poem

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: Someone rode out in search of the right poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Rode is the past tense of ride, travelling on a horse.

clue.text: Lamb's try is possibly luxuriousness

indicators.note: possibly suggests these letters may be arranged another way

parts.note: an iamb is a metrical foot, here with its s

explanation.surface: A poet's attempt at a line in iambs might be self-indulgent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iamb's' looks like a reference to Charles Lamb, but an iamb is a metrical foot and here it only supplies letters. The word comes from Sybaris, a Greek city famous for its love of pleasure.
explanation.definitionFit: The citizens of ancient Sybaris were famed for indulgence, so the word means devotion to luxury and pleasure.
